extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / novice reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and instructions for composing, correcting, sequencing, and analysing news leads and short news stories; focuses on organization, accuracy, tone, and edition-appropriate phrasing for student journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the faults in the organization of the following stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the faults in the organization of the following stories:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify organizational faults such as misplaced facts, lack of logical sequence, weak or missing leads, irrelevant detail placement, failure to prioritize the most important facts, and poor transitions. Use the sample stories to show how organization undermines clarity and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include essential identifying details in leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the age of the person, his place of residence, or similar details necessary to an effective lead are lacking, supply them (paragraphs 100-120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lead should include necessary identifying details (age, residence, occupation, etc.) when they are required for an effective, informative opening. If such details are missing from an item, supply them rather than leaving the lead vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put details in proper sequence for a suicide story
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the following details in proper sequence for a suicide story:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a list of facts about an apparent suicide (time, method, last-known actions, financial or personal background, witness details, whether body was found), arrange them so the lead gives the who/what/when/where/cause concisely, followed by immediate circumstances and then relevant background. Chronology and cause should be clear; avoid burying the key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct leads that need correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct such of the following leads as need correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate leads for accuracy, concision, clarity, and relevance. Rewrite leads that are unclear, overly wordy, ambiguous, sensational, or that omit essential facts. Replace purple prose or misleading phrasing with straightforward, informative opening sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment on and rewrite defective leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on the leads to the following stories, rewriting any that need correction (paragraphs 100-120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide critical commentary identifying specific problems (missing facts, poor emphasis, awkward syntax) and supply rewritten leads that correct those faults. Emphasize clear ordering of facts and suitability for the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose a lead from an outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the lead to the story the outline of which was given on page 290.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform an outline (bullet facts and chronology) into a concise, informative lead: prioritize the most newsworthy fact(s), include necessary identifiers, and craft a single tight opening sentence or paragraph that orients the reader immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write an informal, edition-appropriate lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for Friday afternoon's paper an informal lead to the following story: [characters, ages, marital status, cork leg, hidden cork leg, police called, divorce notice served, address, causes].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor tone and level of formality to the edition (an informal afternoon lead may be more conversational and human-interest oriented). Still include key facts (who, what, when, where, why) but choose a voice and lead shape appropriate to the edition and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain tones and methods used in leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the different tones of the following leads and the writers' methods of gaining their effects (paragraph 119).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how writers create tone: use of direct dialogue, vivid imagery, hyperbole, statistics, ironic juxtaposition, or character sketching. Identify devices (sentence rhythm, detail selection, contrast, quotations) and show how they produce effects like drama, pathos, humour, or outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticize stories for accuracy of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticize the following stories from the standpoint of accuracy of presentation. Rewrite the second. (Paragraphs 122-126.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check factual claims, causal attributions, timelines, and the presence/absence of supporting evidence. Remove or flag speculation, unsupported generalizations, and careless leaps from fact to interpretation. Recast passages to ensure precise, verifiable statements and proper attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purple prose and melodramatic wording in leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid florid or melodramatic language such as 'the beams of the rising sun were struggling to dispel the uncertainties of a winter night' or 'the melting snow-drifts ... ran red with human blood' in news leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News leads should be direct and factual. Identify and eliminate unnecessary poetic flourishes, overwrought metaphors, and sensational phrasing that obscure facts or mislead readers. Prefer plain, precise language that conveys the news efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise and avoid redundancy/awkward phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: What criticism may be made of the following? (example: 'An even one hundred reservations have been made ... and thirty have been made ... No more can be accommodated ... the management will be able to take care of a few more ...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive or clumsy constructions; state numbers and capacities plainly; do not contradict yourself (e.g., saying no more can be accommodated and then that a few more can be taken). Use concise, logically consistent sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor lead content to story type and news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises require writing leads for varied story types (crime, society, obituary, accident, human-interest) and for different editions and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose what to emphasize in the lead (human detail, public impact, chronology, legal status) according to story type and news value. For crimes, prioritize who/what/where/when and legal status; for obituaries, emphasize identity and significance; for human-interest, foreground character detail.
